scope: Complete body read of FitzRoy 135, 212, 218; Fox 175, 184, 197, 261; Whitley 125, 267, compared with Darwin outgoing 310, 319, 327, 314.

read_records.synopsis: Pre-Beagle logistical letter: refuses a midshipman place for young Owen, discusses books, stowage, cabin and delayed sailing.
Voyage-era FitzRoy note joking about Darwin's Rosas/Sierra Ventana campaign, transport, provisions and collections.
Voyage-era answer to Darwin's queries: reports Beagle movements, ship departure plans, people and natural-history map/journal requests.
Early voyage friendship letter: Fox's illness, local politics/news, natural history and encouragement to keep a regular journal.
Fox's illness and Isle of Wight life, insects, Beagle news, offers to forward natural-history stores, and repeated requests for brief news.
Fox reports continued invalidism, Ryde, insects and gull studies, asks where Darwin will go and offers practical help; affectionate natural-history correspondence.
Fox gives family/travel news, wife’s illness and impending confinement, celebrates marriage, discusses Darwin family and return hopes.
Pre-departure Whitley congratulates Darwin on Beagle employment, urges mathematics/navigation study, requests letters and offers help.
Whitley describes Durham academic post, explicitly says he is unmarried/unengaged, reports friends, church and public news, and asks Darwin to write.

assessments.reason: This is a 1831 pre-departure logistical exchange about a midshipman and ship arrangements. Darwin's 310 is a homecoming note about family, England and FitzRoy's government troubles, with no identifiable reply to those particulars.
plausibility_factors: Long-standing close correspondence and shared Beagle experience provide context.
alternatives_or_limits: A lost intervening FitzRoy letter could have supplied a prompt; this pair alone does not identify one.

assessments.reason: Voyage-era correspondence concerns Darwin's Rosas campaign, food, boats and collections in South America; 310 is written after return and contains no matching reply.
plausibility_factors: FitzRoy and Darwin remained in direct contact during the voyage.
alternatives_or_limits: The age of the letter makes it plausible as general context only; no arbitrary lag proves impossibility.

assessments.reason: This is a detailed 1833 voyage answer about Beagle movements and Darwin's requested map/journal, while 310 discusses arrival and reunion rather than those operational matters.
plausibility_factors: The letter documents unusually substantive shared expedition context.
alternatives_or_limits: No specific verbal or topical overlap with 310 identifies it as the prompt.

assessments.reason: Fox's 1832 letter is illness, English news and journal encouragement; 319 instead explains Darwin's immediate London/Shrewsbury/Cambridge itinerary and scientific work. No catalogued phrase or subject anchors a reply.

evidence.quote: I often long so to be with you

plausibility_factors: Affectionate ongoing correspondence could motivate an unpreserved reply.
alternatives_or_limits: Receipt and survival of letters are unknown.

assessments.reason: The catalogued 184 body offers to forward natural-history stores from Fox’s maritime situation and mentions London agents; it does not offer a London or Isle of Wight visit. Therefore its general help cannot be treated as the specific antecedent.

evidence.quote: I have often wished you were with me
though you have offered to come up all the way to London, merely for a flying visit

plausibility_factors: 319 directly records an offer from Fox, creating a concrete overlap in correspondence context.
alternatives_or_limits: 184's offer is stores/help and general visits, not explicitly the London flying visit; sent dates do not establish receipt.

assessments.reason: 197 makes a generic request for brief news and describes Fox’s health and natural-history interests; neither 319 nor 327 answers a distinctive item from this body.

evidence.quote: I had hoped to have heard a few lines from you

plausibility_factors: The request for correspondence is compatible with a later reply.
alternatives_or_limits: Generic requests cannot identify the antecedent; an unlocated Fox letter remains possible.

assessments.reason: 261 contains pregnancy and family news; 319’s daughter joke could reflect family-history continuity, but no evidence proves this catalogued letter was the input.

what relation I am your daughter

plausibility_factors: 261 is the only catalogued Fox input here with immediate marriage/family detail.
alternatives_or_limits: The joke may refer to another Fox letter or shared genealogy; 261 does not identify a daughter.

assessments.reason: 327 covers Cambridge lodging, specimens, Shrewsbury visits and inability to visit Fox; it does not answer 175's health, politics or journal discussion.

evidence.quote: I hope you will not be disgusted at my very stupid letter

alternatives_or_limits: No discriminating overlap identifies 175 as antecedent.

I cannot really spare time at present to go to the Isle of Wight

plausibility_factors: Both letters concern meeting in person and the Isle of Wight/London travel problem.
alternatives_or_limits: 327 likely refers to a recent Fox message, but no catalogued input is explicitly named and 184 is earlier by years.

assessments.reason: 197 makes a generic request for brief news and describes Fox’s health and natural-history interests; neither 319 nor 327 answers a distinctive item from this body.

plausibility_factors: 327 is a natural kind of answer to a request for news.
alternatives_or_limits: 327's own wording suggests a recent exchange not necessarily represented by 197.

assessments.reason: 327 mentions Fox's wife only to say Darwin cannot visit and asks for good annals; it does not respond to 261's pregnancy, illness or marriage advice specifically.

evidence.quote: We therefore now purpose staying at Osmaston thro’ the Winter

plausibility_factors: Both are friendly post-voyage planning correspondence.
alternatives_or_limits: A lost newer Fox letter could explain 327's references.

assessments.reason: 125 is a 1831 pre-departure appointment/advice letter; 314 explicitly acknowledges a marriage-news letter, while 125 contains no marriage news.

evidence.quote: prospect of an employment after your own heart
I was very glad to receive your letter

plausibility_factors: 125 establishes the long friendship and Darwin's departure context.
alternatives_or_limits: The actual marriage-news input is unlocated; 125 cannot be treated as it.

assessments.reason: 267 explicitly says Whitley is unmarried and unengaged in 1835; 314 congratulates him on being married. The catalogued input therefore cannot be the acknowledged marriage-news letter.

evidence.quote: I was very glad to receive your letter

plausibility_factors: 267 is the latest catalogued Whitley letter and documents his life circumstances.
alternatives_or_limits: Whitley's marriage-news letter is not among these records; exact receipt timing is unavailable.

findings: FitzRoy 135, 212 and 218 are contextual correspondence only for 310: their specific subjects do not recur in Darwin’s homecoming letter. Years of direct Beagle contact make an old letter an unlikely direct prompt after return, but do not prove impossibility; 310’s own account of the final days aboard is closer context.

Fox 319 explicitly answers an unlocated letter offering a London flying visit. Fox 184 offers stores/help and mentions London agents but contains no visit offer, so it is not a specific match. Fox 197 is generic news-seeking correspondence; 327’s meeting language does not establish which incoming letter preceded it.
Whitley 314’s marriage acknowledgment rules out 125 and 267 as the specific marriage-news input: 125 predates the voyage and 267 says he was unmarried/unengaged.
No assessment infers receipt from sent date or Darwin’s availability from an incoming author’s acknowledgment.
limitations: The review covers the nine specified incoming bodies and four specified outgoing bodies in the packet; missing, unlocated, or lost letters may contain actual prompts.
Evidence offsets index the packet’s original paragraph text, including retained punctuation and spacing; editorial summaries/footnotes were not treated as body evidence.
Shared topics and continuity support historical plausibility judgments only; they do not attest antecedent identity.
